concept_card.core_rule: A two-way table organises counts for two categorical variables; comparing row or column percentages helps judge whether the variables may be related.

hint_levels.template: Decide whether row percentages or column percentages answer the question.
Compare proportions, not just raw counts, when group sizes differ.
A two-way table is a grid for fair comparison: totals tell you which percentages are meaningful.

worked_example.question: In a survey, 30 of 50 students who play sport prefer early classes, while 12 of 40 students who do not play sport prefer early classes. Compare the groups.
worked_example.answer: Sport players: $60\%$; non-sport players: $30\%$. Early-class preference appears higher among sport players.
worked_example.explanation: Work from the defining rule or model, then interpret the result in context.

steps.result: Sport: 30 early and 20 not early; no sport: 12 early and 28 not early.
The preference is higher in the sport group, but this does not prove sport causes the preference.

learning_objectives: I can construct and interpret two-way tables.
I can compare categorical groups using appropriate percentages.
I can discuss possible relationships without overstating causation.

explanation_sections.heading: Categorical bivariate data
explanation_sections.body: Two-way tables show how two categorical variables combine, such as transport mode and year level or device type and app preference.

explanation_sections.heading: Percentages for fair comparison
explanation_sections.body: Raw counts can mislead when group totals differ. Use percentages within the relevant row or column.

explanation_sections.heading: Quick check: fair percentages
explanation_sections.body:
1. Why can raw counts mislead in a two-way table?
2. When comparing groups, should percentages usually be within rows/columns or over the whole table?
Answers: group totals may differ; use the relevant row or column denominator.

key_vocabulary.definition: A table that organises counts for two categorical variables.
A percentage calculated using the total of a row.
A variable whose values are categories or groups.

common_mistakes: Comparing raw counts when group sizes are different.
Using the wrong total for a percentage.
real_world_connections: Two-way tables are used in surveys, marketing, medical risk comparisons, school reports and public policy analysis.

additional_worked_examples.question: Core/application: In a sample, 36 of 90 bus users and 24 of 60 train users are late at least once. Compare lateness proportions.
additional_worked_examples.answer: Both are $40\%$, so the lateness proportions are equal.

additional_worked_examples.question: Extension/error analysis: A student says bus users are later because 36 late bus users is more than 24 late train users. Explain.
additional_worked_examples.answer: The group sizes differ, so proportions must be compared rather than raw counts.

steps.result: There are 90 bus users and 60 train users.
The data do not show a higher lateness rate for bus users.

guided_practice.question: A table shows 18 of 60 Year 10 students and 24 of 80 Year 11 students cycle to school. Which year level has the higher cycling proportion?
guided_practice.answer: Both are $30\%$, so the proportions are equal.

steps.result: The proportions are the same despite different counts.

independent_practice.question: Construct a two-way table from these records: Year 10—bus, bus, car, cycle, cycle, bus; Year 11—bus, car, car, cycle, car, bus. Calculate within-year transport percentages and discuss a possible relationship cautiously.
independent_practice.answer: Year 10 counts: bus 3, car 1, cycle 2; Year 11: bus 2, car 3, cycle 1. Percentages are Year 10: $50\%,16.7\%,33.3\%$ and Year 11: $33.3\%,50\%,16.7\%$. The sample suggests transport mix may differ by year level, but 12 records are too few for a strong population inference.

success_criteria: I can construct and interpret two-way tables.
I can compare categorical groups using appropriate percentages.
I can discuss possible relationships without overstating causation.

habit_challenges.description: Write the denominator beside every percentage from a two-way table.

topics.name: Bivariate statistical investigations
topics.achievement_standard_text: Students plan and conduct statistical investigations involving bivariate data and evaluate limitations.
topics.content_descriptor_text: plan and conduct statistical investigations of situations that involve bivariate data; evaluate and report findings with consideration of limitations of any inferences

elaborations.text: planning investigations involving two variables such as housing affordability, health, environment or school contexts
evaluating findings with attention to limitations of inferences and possible confounding variables

concept_card.core_rule: A bivariate statistical investigation studies two variables together; conclusions should match the data type, sampling method, analysis and limitations.

hint_levels.template: Name both variables and classify each as numerical or categorical before planning displays.
Choose scatterplots for two numerical variables and two-way tables for two categorical variables.
A good investigation report has a claim, evidence and limitation in the same paragraph.

worked_example.question: Plan an investigation into whether screen time is associated with sleep duration for Year 10 students. Name variables, display and one limitation.
worked_example.answer: Variables: screen time and sleep duration, both numerical. Use a scatterplot. A limitation is self-reported data may be inaccurate.
worked_example.explanation: Work from the defining rule or model, then interpret the result in context.

steps.result: Is screen time associated with sleep duration for Year 10 students?
Both variables are numerical, measured in hours.
Use a scatterplot; self-reporting may introduce error.

learning_objectives: I can plan a bivariate investigation with suitable variables and displays.
I can analyse paired data using scatterplots or two-way tables as appropriate.
I can report findings with limitations and possible confounding variables.

explanation_sections.heading: Planning with two variables
explanation_sections.body: The question must make clear which two variables are being investigated and what kind of relationship is being explored.

explanation_sections.heading: Reporting responsibly
explanation_sections.body: Reports should include data collection method, display choice, summary of evidence, conclusion and limitations of inference.

explanation_sections.heading: Quick check: bivariate investigation quality
explanation_sections.body:
1. What must a bivariate question identify?
2. Name one limitation that should be reported.
Answers: the two variables and the relationship being explored; examples include sample method, sample size, measurement quality or inference limits.

key_vocabulary.definition: Data involving two variables measured or recorded for each case.
A third variable that may affect the relationship between the two variables being studied.
A weakness or boundary in how far the findings can be trusted or generalised.

common_mistakes: Collecting two variables but analysing each separately instead of together.
Ignoring sample size, sampling method or confounding variables in the conclusion.
real_world_connections: Bivariate investigations support research in health, economics, education, environmental science and product design.

additional_worked_examples.question: Core/application: Plan a bivariate investigation of height and arm span. Name the variables and display.
additional_worked_examples.answer: Variables: height and arm span, both numerical; use a scatterplot.

steps.result: Is height associated with arm span?
A scatterplot suits two numerical variables.

additional_worked_examples.question: Extension/error analysis: A report on homework time and grades ignores prior achievement. Why is this a limitation?
additional_worked_examples.answer: Prior achievement may be a confounding variable affecting both homework time and grades.

steps.result: It may influence both variables in the study.
The inference about homework and grades is weaker.

guided_practice.question: Choose a display for investigating whether commute distance is associated with commute time.
guided_practice.answer: A scatterplot, because both variables are numerical and the question asks about association.

steps.result: Scatterplot shows association between two numerical variables.

independent_practice.question: Plan a complete bivariate investigation of exercise hours and stress score: specify population, sample, paired measurements, ethics, display and analysis; then give a report template that evaluates inference strength and possible confounders.
independent_practice.answer: Use a fair sample from the stated population, collect anonymous paired weekly exercise hours and a clearly defined stress score with consent, and use a scatterplot to describe strength, direction, linearity and outliers. Report the observed association, sample method and size, measurement limits and uncertainty; discuss sleep, workload and health as confounders and do not claim exercise causes the stress pattern.

success_criteria: I can plan a bivariate investigation with suitable variables and displays.
I can analyse paired data using scatterplots or two-way tables as appropriate.
I can report findings with limitations and possible confounding variables.

habit_challenges.description: Finish each bivariate report with one claim, one piece of evidence and one limitation.

topics.name: Conditional probability language
topics.achievement_standard_text: Students apply conditional probability to solve problems involving compound events.
topics.content_descriptor_text: use the language of 'if ... then', 'given', 'of' and 'knowing that' to describe and interpret situations involving conditional probability

elaborations.text: using language such as if, then, given, of and knowing that to interpret conditional probability situations
identifying dependent and independent relationships in probability tables and event descriptions

concept_card.core_rule: Conditional probability restricts the sample space: $P(A\mid B)$ means the probability of A among outcomes where B is already known to have occurred.

hint_levels.template: Translate 'given' or 'knowing that' into a smaller denominator.
Use the condition to narrow the sample space before counting favourable outcomes.
Conditional probability is like entering a room after one fact is known; you count only people still in that room.

worked_example.question: In a group of 50 students, 20 study Chemistry, 18 study Physics and 8 study both. Find $P(\text{Physics}\mid\text{Chemistry})$.
worked_example.explanation: Work from the defining rule or model, then interpret the result in context.

steps.result: Given Chemistry means the denominator is the 20 Chemistry students.

steps.instruction: Identify favourable outcomes within that group.

learning_objectives: I can translate conditional probability language into the correct denominator.
I can calculate conditional probabilities from tables, trees or counts.
I can distinguish dependent and independent events.

explanation_sections.heading: Restricting the sample space
explanation_sections.body: The condition tells us which outcomes remain possible. Probabilities are then calculated within this reduced group.

explanation_sections.heading: Dependent and independent events
explanation_sections.body: If knowing B changes the probability of A, the events are dependent. If it does not, they are independent.

explanation_sections.heading: Quick check: condition changes denominator
explanation_sections.body:
1. In $P(A\mid B)$, which group becomes the sample space?
2. Why are $P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$ usually different?
Answers: the outcomes where B has occurred; the denominators are different.

key_vocabulary.definition: The probability of an event when another event is known to have occurred.
The set of possible outcomes being considered.
Events where knowing one event occurred does not change the probability of the other.

common_mistakes: Using the total population as the denominator after a condition is given.
Confusing $P(A\mid B)$ with $P(B\mid A)$.
real_world_connections: Conditional probability is used in medical testing, risk analysis, recommendation systems and quality control.

additional_worked_examples.question: Core/application: In a group of 60 students, 24 play music, 18 play sport and 9 do both. Find $P(\text{music}\mid\text{sport})$.

steps.result: Given sport means the denominator is 18.

additional_worked_examples.question: Extension/error analysis: A student treats $P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$ as always equal. Give a counterexample.
additional_worked_examples.answer: If 9 of 18 sport players play music but 9 of 24 music players play sport, the probabilities are $1/2$ and $3/8$, not equal.

steps.result: The denominator changes with the condition.

guided_practice.question: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue counters. One counter is drawn and not replaced. If the first counter was red, find the probability the second is red.

steps.result: One red has already been removed.
There are 4 red counters out of 7 counters left.

independent_practice.question: Translate among these forms and identify the conditioned denominator: 'netball given sport', 'of sport players, those who play netball', 'knowing that a student plays sport', and an if–then description. Explain why reversing the condition changes the question.
independent_practice.answer: All first three restrict the sample space to sport players and ask what fraction also play netball; an if–then version is 'if the selected student plays sport, then what is the chance they play netball?' Reversing to sport given netball restricts to netball players, so the denominator changes.

success_criteria: I can translate conditional probability language into the correct denominator.
I can calculate conditional probabilities from tables, trees or counts.
I can distinguish dependent and independent events.

habit_challenges.description: Circle the condition and write the reduced denominator before calculating.

topics.name: Conditional probability simulations
topics.achievement_standard_text: Students design and conduct simulations involving conditional probability using digital tools.
topics.content_descriptor_text: design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations using digital tools to model conditional probability and interpret results

elaborations.text: using digital tools to model conditional probability situations and interpret repeated-trial results
testing intuitions about chance events that may or may not be independent

concept_card.core_rule: A conditional probability simulation must define the condition, count only trials where the condition occurs and estimate the desired probability from that restricted set of trials.

hint_levels.template: Record both the total trials and the number of trials that satisfy the condition.
Estimate the probability using favourable conditioned trials divided by all conditioned trials.
A simulation is a filter: first filter to the 'given' cases, then calculate within that filtered group.

worked_example.question: A simulation draws two counters without replacement from a bag with 4 red and 6 blue counters. In 5000 trials, the first counter was red in 1995 trials; of those, the second was blue in 1338 trials. Estimate $P(\text{blue second}\mid\text{red first})$.
worked_example.explanation: Work from the defining rule or model, then interpret the result in context.

steps.result: Only the 1995 trials where the first counter was red are used.

learning_objectives: I can design simulations for conditional probability.
I can calculate estimates using only conditioned trials.
I can compare simulated results with theoretical reasoning where possible.

explanation_sections.heading: Designing the simulation
explanation_sections.body: A good simulation states the random process, the condition, the event being estimated and how many trials will be run.

explanation_sections.heading: Interpreting results
explanation_sections.body: Simulation estimates vary. More trials usually reduce fluctuation, but the result should still be interpreted as an estimate.

explanation_sections.heading: Quick check: simulation design
explanation_sections.body:
1. What four things should a conditional-probability simulation state?
2. Why do more trials usually help?
Answers: the random process, condition, event and number of trials; more trials reduce random fluctuation.

key_vocabulary.definition: A trial that satisfies the given condition and is included in the conditional probability estimate.
A repeated model of a chance process used to estimate probabilities.
A probability estimated from observed or simulated relative frequency.

common_mistakes: Dividing by all simulation trials instead of only trials satisfying the condition.
Forgetting to state the condition before interpreting the result.
real_world_connections: Simulations help estimate conditional risks in queues, games, reliability testing, medical screening and finance.

additional_worked_examples.question: Core/application: In a simulation of 3000 families with two children, at least one child was a girl in 2256 trials; both children were girls in 742 of those. Estimate $P(\text{two girls}\mid\text{at least one girl})$.

steps.result: Only 2256 trials had at least one girl.

additional_worked_examples.question: Extension/error analysis: A student divides 742 by 3000 in the previous simulation. Explain the error.
additional_worked_examples.answer: That estimates $P(\text{two girls and at least one girl})$, not the conditional probability given at least one girl.

guided_practice.question: A digital spinner simulation records 2000 two-spin trials. The first spin lands on A in 520 trials; among those, the second spin lands on A in 126 trials. Estimate $P(\text{second A}\mid\text{first A})$.

steps.result: There are 520 trials where first spin was A.

independent_practice.question: Design and conduct or specify a digital simulation to estimate $P(\text{two girls}\mid\text{at least one girl})$ for two-child families. Define random coding, condition, counted event, trial totals and assumptions; explain how the conditioned denominator is used.
independent_practice.answer: Model each child independently as G/B with probability $1/2$, generate two outcomes per trial, retain only GG, GB and BG, and estimate with $\text{GG count}/\text{retained count}$. Report total and retained trials and compare with theoretical $1/3$. The result depends on the binary, equal-probability, independent-birth model assumptions.

success_criteria: I can design simulations for conditional probability.
I can calculate estimates using only conditioned trials.
I can compare simulated results with theoretical reasoning where possible.

habit_challenges.description: In simulation results, write the filtered denominator before calculating the conditional estimate.
